extracted.intended_audience: general readers, policymakers, development practitioners, and potential borrower countries interested in the Inter-American Development Bank's mandate, governance, and funding priorities
extracted.subtask_description: Describes the Inter-American Development Bank's mission, governance, financing instruments, eligibility rules, strategic objectives, priority focus areas, performance metrics, and critiques — useful for understanding what the Bank funds and how it operates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility for loans / Borrowing members
rubrics_metrics.description: Only the 26 borrowing countries are able to receive loans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Bank is owned by 48 sovereign states (shareholders/members) but only borrowing members (listed on the page) may receive IDB loans; membership status (borrowing vs non-borrowing) therefore determines eligibility to be a recipient of financial operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority areas / Seven focus areas
rubrics_metrics.description: According to the Bank's latest institutional strategy, it works in seven focus areas: 1. biodiversity, natural capital, and climate action; 2. gender equality and inclusion of diverse population groups; 3. institutional capacity, rule of law, and citizen security; 4. social protection and human capital development; 5. sustainable, resilient, and inclusive infrastructure; 6. productive development and innovation through the private sector; 7. regional integration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These focus areas define the thematic priorities that the IDB aims to support when approving loans, investments, technical assistance, and other operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional strategy core objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: The strategy's three core objectives are reducing poverty and inequality, addressing climate change, and bolstering sustainable growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board-approved institutional strategy and reforms guide the Bank's selection and design of operations; related approvals (e.g., doubling IDB Invest capital, IDB Lab replenishment) are intended to increase impact in service of these objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of support and instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: The IDB supports development by lending to governments and sub-national agencies, developing new financial tools, creating enabling conditions for private-sector-led growth, convening and aligning countries, bridging the region with the rest of the world, and providing technical assistance; it also works alongside IDB Invest (private-sector lending, mobilization, advisory) and IDB Lab (entrepreneurship and venture capital).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Project or program proposals can be funded via sovereign-guaranteed loans, IDB Invest commitments for private sector support, IDB Lab approvals for innovation ventures, or technical cooperation; examples: 92 sovereign-guaranteed loan projects for $12.7 billion in 2023; IDB Invest mobilized private resources including $5.3 billion in 2023.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial resources and capital structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The callable capital pledged by the 22 non-borrowing members functions as a guarantee for bonds that the IDB sells; ordinary capital (about $101 billion) comprises paid-in capital plus callable subscriptions, with 4.3% paid in and 95.7% callable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This capital structure secures a triple-A credit rating, enabling the Bank to raise funds by issuing bonds at commercial rates and thus lend to borrowing countries at rates similar to those charged to large corporate borrowers. Non-borrowing members provide guarantees (callable capital) rather than immediate cash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferred creditor status
rubrics_metrics.description: The IDB has preferred creditor status, meaning that borrowers will repay loans to the IDB before repaying other obligations to other lenders such as commercial banks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred creditor status affects perceived repayment risk and the Bank's lending terms and is cited as a factor reducing default risk despite borrowers being developing countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governance and voting power
rubrics_metrics.description: The Bank is governed by a Board of Governors (usually finance ministers or senior economic officials) and voting power is determined by each member's shareholding (subscription to ordinary capital); developing (borrowing) countries are the majority shareholders as a group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governance arrangements (annual meetings, Board approvals) determine major policy decisions, capital increases, and leadership; examples include the US holding 30% of shares while Latin American and Caribbean countries combined hold 50.02%.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance and impact measurement metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: The IDB reports quantitative metrics of activity and impact such as number and value of approved sovereign-guaranteed loan projects, IDB Invest activity and mobilized private resources, and the share of approvals that support sustainable economic growth (e.g., 76% of IDB loan approvals, 94% of IDB Invest commitments, 96% of IDB Lab approvals claimed to support sustainable economic growth in 2024).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These internal measures are used to track the Bank’s output and claimed contributions to strategic objectives and can influence future resourcing and strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital increases and business model reforms as funding criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board can approve capital increases and business model reforms to expand financing capacity (e.g., a $70 billion ordinary capital increase agreed in 2010; a 2024 recapitalization and a new 'originate to share' business model for IDB Invest; a stated intention to increase financing capacity by $130 billion over a decade).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such capital and business-model changes affect the Bank’s ability to mobilize resources and prioritize sectors or instruments (e.g., more capital for IDB Invest to mobilize private finance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental and social impact concerns / safeguards (criticisms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil society groups and the Bank Information Center claim that IDB-funded operations may have adverse impacts on local environments and indigenous peoples, citing environmental and social damage and concerns about effects on local economies and democratic reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These criticisms imply the importance of environmental and social risk assessment, consultation with affected communities, and safeguards in project design and approval; the page documents these concerns as a factor that can affect legitimacy and acceptance of IDB operations.
